messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tailor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 79

He is 33, a single African man who works as a tailor, and before the bombing he describes his life in small, steady routines. He opens his shop early, sweeps the cement floor, oils the machine when it sticks, and spends long afternoons bent over hems and cuffs while customers come and go. He likes precise work. He says sewing gives him a way to make order from loose fabric. In his telling, this is how life feels then too: not easy, but manageable, held together by habit, prayer, and work.

The day of the attack begins like any other. He is in the market area near his shop, carrying fabric he has just bought for a customer who wants matching outfits sewn for a family celebration. He remembers the colors of the cloth more clearly than anything that happens a few minutes before the blast. Then there is a violent sound, a force that seems to tear the air apart, and the sensation of being thrown sideways. For a few seconds he cannot understand what has happened. When he opens his eyes, the market is smoke, dust, screaming, and broken bodies. He tastes blood and grit. One of his ears rings so loudly he thinks he has gone deaf.

He crawls behind a stall frame and stays there, frozen, while people run in every direction. He sees a woman stumbling with part of her dress burned away. He sees a man on the ground who does not move again. He cannot stop staring at a child’s shoe lying by itself in the dirt. Later, when he talks about that day, he does not tell the story in a smooth line. He stops abruptly, rubs his hands together, and goes quiet, as if his body has returned to that place before his words can follow.

In the days after, he goes back to the damaged shop because he does not know what else to do. He tells himself he is lucky to be alive, that other people lost more. But the world no longer feels ordinary. Every sharp noise makes him jerk so hard he drops his scissors or snaps the thread he is feeding through a needle. When a motorcycle backfires outside, his chest clamps tight and he is instantly back in the market, smelling smoke. He begins scanning every customer who enters, watching their hands, their bags, how long they linger. If someone leaves a parcel unattended, he cannot concentrate until it is gone.

Sleep becomes a nightly battle. He lies down exhausted but resists closing his eyes because he knows what waits for him there. When he does sleep, he wakes drenched in sweat, hearing the blast again or seeing the ground scattered with bodies. Some nights he wakes shouting and sits upright, disoriented, reaching for the wall as if he must steady himself. By morning he feels beaten down, but he still goes to the shop. He says work used to calm him; now even work has changed. He used to enjoy customers chatting while he measured and pinned fabric. Now the sound of many voices at once makes him tense. He keeps the radio off. He prefers the door partly closed. He sits where he can see the street.

As months pass, his life grows smaller. He avoids the market unless he has no choice, even though this means paying more for cloth elsewhere and losing money he cannot spare. He turns down jobs that require him to attend crowded ceremonies for fittings. Friends invite him out, but he gives excuses. He does not want to answer questions, and he cannot bear places where people laugh loudly and chairs scrape suddenly across the floor. He is single, and he says there was a time when he imagined marrying soon, but now he keeps himself apart. He feels detached even from relatives he loves. When they sit together, he often seems physically present but far away, watching the doorway, missing parts of the conversation.

What troubles him almost as much as fear is the change in how he sees himself. He used to think of himself as patient, dependable, and strong. Now he is quick to anger. If a customer complains about a delay, he feels a surge of heat and has to bite back harsh words. At times he is ashamed of how frightened he is. At other times he is convinced nowhere is safe and no planning matters because death can arrive without warning in the middle of an ordinary morning.

He still sews every day. He presses seams carefully, rethreads needles, marks chalk lines with practiced hands. From the outside, his life can look intact. But he lives as though the explosion is not finished, as though some part of him remains under that broken market stall, braced for the next blast.
